name: Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma
aliases: extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue

clinicalPearls: An indolent marginal-zone B-cell lymphoma arising in extranodal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, most commonly the stomach but also lung, salivary gland, thyroid, ocular adnexa and skin
Chronic antigenic stimulation drives the disease, classically Helicobacter pylori in gastric MALT lymphoma and autoimmune conditions such as Sjogren syndrome or Hashimoto thyroiditis at other sites
Early-stage H. pylori-positive gastric disease frequently regresses with eradication therapy alone, making this a lymphoma treatable with antibiotics
The translocation t(11;18) fusing API2 and MALT1 predicts a lower likelihood of response to H. pylori eradication and tends to remain localised
Lymphoepithelial lesions, where neoplastic B cells infiltrate and disrupt glandular epithelium, are a histological hallmark
The immunophenotype is CD20-positive with CD5, CD10, CD23 and cyclin D1 negativity, helping to distinguish it from other small B-cell lymphomas
Localised H. pylori-negative or non-responding disease is managed with radiotherapy or anti-CD20 targeted therapy, and disseminated disease with chemoimmunotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: MALT lymphoma develops at sites of acquired lymphoid tissue generated by chronic infection or autoimmune inflammation. Persistent antigenic drive, exemplified by Helicobacter pylori in the stomach, sustains T-cell-dependent proliferation of marginal-zone B cells; early in the disease this dependence explains why eradicating the antigenic stimulus can lead to regression. Over time the acquisition of genetic changes, notably translocations such as t(11;18) that generate the API2-MALT1 fusion and constitutively activate NF-kappaB signalling, renders the lymphoma antigen-independent and unlikely to respond to eradication. The infiltrate expands the marginal zone, colonises follicles and produces lymphoepithelial lesions within glandular structures.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive lymphoid hyperplasia or chronic gastritis with lymphoid follicles
Follicular lymphoma involving an extranodal site
Mantle cell lymphoma (including lymphomatous polyposis of the gut)
Nodal or splenic marginal zone lymphoma with extranodal spread
additionalInvestigations: Endoscopy with multiple mucosal biopsies for gastric disease, including testing for Helicobacter pylori
Immunohistochemistry showing CD20-positive, CD5/CD10/CD23/cyclin D1-negative marginal-zone B cells with lymphoepithelial lesions
FISH or molecular testing for t(11;18) API2-MALT1 to guide therapy
Staging imaging and, for gastric disease, assessment of depth of invasion and regional nodes
Autoimmune serology (e.g. for Sjogren syndrome or Hashimoto thyroiditis) at relevant sites
Bone marrow examination and blood counts for staging
redFlags: Transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma indicated by a rapidly enlarging mass, ulceration or rising lactate dehydrogenase
Gastrointestinal bleeding, obstruction or perforation from gastric disease
Failure of gastric lymphoma to regress after documented H. pylori eradication
Orbital or airway compromise from bulky extranodal disease
reference.prognosis: The overall prognosis is excellent with prolonged survival; early gastric disease often achieves durable remission after H. pylori eradication, while t(11;18)-positive tumours are less likely to respond to eradication but usually remain localised, and the main adverse event is transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma.
pitfalls: Failing to test for and eradicate Helicobacter pylori in gastric disease
Expecting eradication to work in t(11;18)-positive tumours
Discontinuing surveillance too early, as regression after eradication can be slow
Missing multifocal or disseminated disease by not staging adequately
Overlooking transformation to aggressive lymphoma in a changing lesion
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on marginal zone lymphomas
management: Treatment is driven mainly by stage and site rather than a single algorithm, and should be planned with a haemato oncology multidisciplinary team

Localised (stage I/II) gastric disease associated with H. pylori and without the t(11;18) translocation is treated first line with H. pylori eradication antibiotic therapy, giving excellent long term outcomes
If gastric disease is H. pylori negative, carries t(11;18), or fails to regress after documented eradication, radiotherapy is the preferred treatment for localised disease
Ocular adnexal disease is primarily treated with low dose radiotherapy, with antibiotic therapy targeting Chlamydophila psittaci as a less durable alternative that has been studied for this site
Hepatitis C associated disease, even at advanced stage, should have antiviral therapy for the HCV infection considered before other systemic treatment, since it may itself produce lymphoma regression
Other extranodal sites such as salivary gland, thyroid, lung, and skin follow the same general principle of radiotherapy or site appropriate local therapy for localised disease
Surgery's role is mainly diagnostic biopsy and management of site specific complications such as bleeding, obstruction, or perforation, rather than primary curative treatment
Advanced stage disease behaves as an indolent lymphoma, and close observation is appropriate until symptoms, signs, or organ impairment develop
Systemic therapy is reserved for relapsed or refractory disease after antibiotic or radiotherapy, or for advanced or symptomatic disease, and its approach mirrors follicular lymphoma management

Systemic options include single agent alkylating agents, single agent anti-CD20 antibody therapy, purine analog based regimens, and combination chemoimmunotherapy, with combination approaches giving higher response but greater toxicity

For marginal zone lymphoma as a category, Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors and a PI3K inhibitor are approved options in the relapsed or refractory setting, and CD19 directed CAR T-cell therapy continues to be explored in the third line and beyond

Monitoring should watch for transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly an ABC-like diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and any rapidly enlarging mass, ulceration, or new organ impairment should prompt rebiopsy

Staging and monitoring includes cross sectional imaging of chest, abdomen, and pelvis, imaging of the neck and orbits, bone marrow biopsy consideration for multifocal disease, and evaluation of the gastric mucosa in non-gastric disease

All patients should be managed through a multidisciplinary team with site specific specialist input, and referred promptly for rebiopsy and re-staging if eradication fails to produce regression or transformation is suspected
